stem: A federal contractor already runs its workloads on AWS. Its authorization requires a FedRAMP High service, and AWS must be the only party that operates the inference infrastructure and processes prompts and outputs. Which way of calling Claude fits these requirements?

options.text: Claude Platform on AWS, since it is billed through AWS Marketplace and authenticates with IAM.
options.why: AWS handles billing and identity there, but Anthropic operates the platform and processes inference data, so AWS is not the only operator.

options.text: Claude in Amazon Bedrock, called through the SDK's Bedrock client with AWS credentials.
options.why: Bedrock runs Claude on AWS-operated infrastructure with AWS as the data processor, which is the offering the docs point to for FedRAMP High and similar requirements.

options.text: The first-party Claude API, reached from the company's VPC over a private network link.
options.why: A private network path changes how traffic reaches the API, not who operates the inference infrastructure or processes the data.

options.text: The first-party Claude API with inference_geo set to "us" on every request.
options.why: Inference geo controls where inference runs geographically; it does not make AWS the operator or data processor.

explanation: Claude can be reached on AWS in two different ways. Claude in Amazon Bedrock is an AWS-native service: AWS operates the inference stack and processes the data, which is why the docs recommend it for FedRAMP High, IL4/IL5 or HIPAA-ready needs and whenever AWS must be the sole data processor. Claude Platform on AWS is Anthropic-operated, with AWS providing IAM authentication and Marketplace billing, and it tracks first-party features more closely. Choose by who must operate the stack and process data, then check that platform's feature list.
reference: Claude API docs — Claude Platform on AWS (versus Amazon Bedrock); Claude in Amazon Bedrock

stem: A receipts app uploads phone photos to storage, where a thumbnailer saves them as JPEG. A worker later reloads each image, compresses it again as a low-quality JPEG to save bandwidth, and sends it to Claude to extract line items. Claude often misreads small printed prices. What should the team change first?

options.text: Send each image in four more copies in the same request so Claude can cross-check the prices.
options.why: Duplicates add tokens and payload without restoring detail that repeated compression already destroyed.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so Claude has more room to reason about hard-to-read digits.
options.why: max_tokens caps output length; it cannot recover detail missing from the image Claude receives.

options.text: Encode once from the original photo, cropped and resized, with settings that keep text legible.
options.why: Each lossy compression pass adds artifacts that make small text hard to read; one pass from the original, with cropping and pre-resizing, keeps text clear and requests small.

options.text: Send the full-resolution original every time so that the API itself never has to resize anything.
options.why: Images above the model's native resolution are downscaled anyway, so this raises payload size and latency without guaranteeing legible text.

explanation: Lossy compression such as JPEG reduces request size and latency, but artifacts accumulate with multiple compression passes and can make text hard to read. Encode once from the source, pre-resize to the model's native resolution and crop to the relevant region, and inspect the actual images the application sends to the API.
reference: Claude API docs — Vision (image quality guidance; resolution and token cost)

stem: A chat service built on the Messages API runs on several load-balanced workers. Each worker keeps one in-memory messages list that it appends every incoming turn to. Users report that Claude mentions other customers' orders, and conversations lose context when a later request lands on a different worker. What is the best fix?

options.text: Enable sticky sessions on the load balancer so that each user always reaches the same worker.
options.why: Stickiness may reduce lost context, but users on one worker still share its single list, so the leak remains, and history is lost when a worker restarts.

options.text: Add a system prompt rule telling Claude never to mention details from other customers' conversations.
options.why: The other customers' data is still sent in the request; an instruction does not stop it from being exposed, and the cross-worker loss is untouched.

options.text: Send only the newest user message on each request so no history can leak between customers.
options.why: The API is stateless, so dropping history removes all conversational context; the problem is shared history, not history itself.

options.text: Store each conversation's history in a shared store keyed by conversation ID and load only that one per request.
options.why: Per-conversation history in a shared store isolates customers from each other, and any worker can load the right history for the request it receives.

explanation: The Messages API is stateless: the application decides exactly which history each request carries. Session hygiene in a multi-user service means scoping history to one conversation, keying it by a conversation or session ID, and keeping it in a store every worker can reach, so no request ever carries another user's turns and any worker can resume a conversation.
reference: Claude API docs — Messages API (multi-turn conversations); Context windows
